newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish IVO to send last nuclear load to Russia.
newsitem.headline: Finnish IVO to send last nuclear load to Russia.

text.p: After sending nuclear waste to Russia for 15 years, Finnish power producer Imatran Voima Oy said on Tuesday it will send one last shipment and then find a way to dispose of the waste itself.

The practice of returning nuclear waste to Russia is ending in accordance with a 1994 decision of the Finnish parliament banning the import and export of spent nuclear fuel as of the beginning of 1997.

State-owned Imatran Voima (IVO) said in a statement received late on Monday that a Russian train had arrived at its Loviisa nuclear power plant east of Helsinki to fetch the last-ever load of spent fuel to be sent to Russia.
"This is the fifteenth and, at the same time, the last return shipment of used uranium fuel from Loviisa to the Mayak reprocessing plant (in Russia)," IVO said.

During the next few days, the plant will begin loading about 29 tonnes of uranium packed in eight thick-walled steel vessels onto the train for shipment in the next few weeks to the Mayak plant at Chelyabinsk in the southern Urals, IVO said.
Since 1981, the Loviisa plant has sent 15 shipments, amounting to 307 tonnes of uranium, to the reprocessing plant, the company said.
IVO's waste disposal agreement with the Russians dates from the 1970s when IVO contracted to have the Soviet-designed power plant built.
The Loviisa plant is one of Finland's two nuclear power installations, each with two reactors, which together generate about 30 percent of the country's electricity.

The other installation is the Olkiluoto nuclear power plant situated on the southwest coast and owned by the industry-backed Teollisuuden Voima (TVO) power company, which says it has never exported nuclear waste.
With the convenience of exporting the radioactive waste to Russia now ending, IVO is now searching for a suitable location for a final repository in Finland.
"IVO has already prepared for final disposal of used nuclear fuel in Finnish bedrock together with Teollisuuden Voima," IVO said.

Three sites for the disposal unit are being investigated, at Eurajoki in the southwest, Aanekoski in central Finland and Kuhmo in the northeast, IVO purchase manager Ossi Koskivirta said. A site is expected to be chosen in 2000.
The cost of the final repository has been estimated at around 3 billion markka, Koskivirta said.
Imatran Voima is 95.6 percent state-owned. In 1995 the company's profits before extraordinary items came to 1.13 billion markka, up from 347 million the previous year.
After reporting January-August profits of 1.16 billion, the company said in October that its 1996 profit would be better than in 1996.
The government plans to float part of the company.
